content: The human body harbors a vast number of bacteria, many of which perform essential functions that are critical for human survival. These bacteria, which are expected to be present and typically do not cause disease under normal conditions, are referred to as the normal flora. It is estimated that between 500 and 1,000 different bacterial species inhabit the human body. Bacterial cells are significantly smaller than human cells, and their numbers in the body are approximately ten times greater than human cells, with about 1,000 trillion bacterial cells compared to 100 trillion human cells. Normal flora are found on all surfaces of the body exposed to the external environment, including the skin, eyes, mouth, nose, small intestine, and colon. However, the majority of these bacteria reside in the large intestine. Certain areas of the body, such as the blood, urine, brain, and lungs, are normally sterile, although they can become infected under specific circumstances. The bacteria in the digestive tract, collectively known as gut flora, play a crucial role in breaking down nutrients, such as carbohydrates, that humans cannot digest on their own. Most of these gut bacteria are anaerobes, meaning they thrive in environments devoid of oxygen. While the normal flora is generally harmless, some of these bacteria can act as opportunistic pathogens, causing disease when the immune system is compromised. For example, Escherichia coli (E. coli), a bacterium commonly found in the colon, is a well-studied model organism. However, certain mutated strains, such as E. coli O157:H7, can cause severe disease. In the mouth, bacteria such as Actinomyces viscosus and A. naeslundii are components of dental plaque. If plaque is not removed through brushing, it hardens into tartar (calculus). These bacteria also produce acids that erode tooth enamel, leading to tooth decay. The vaginal microbiota predominantly consists of various Lactobacillus species. While it was previously believed that Lactobacillus acidophilus was the most common species, research has shown that Lactobacillus iners and Lactobacillus crispatus are more prevalent. Other species, such as Lactobacillus delbrueckii and Lactobacillus gasseri, are also present. Disruptions in the vaginal flora can result in bacterial vaginosis. Bacteria are essential for maintaining human health, but some species can also pose significant health risks by causing diseases. Large populations of bacteria reside on the skin and in the digestive tract, where their growth can be influenced by factors such as warmth and sweat. These bacteria contribute to body odor and may play a role in acne. The more than 500 bacterial species in the human gut provide numerous benefits, including the synthesis of vitamins like folic acid, vitamin K, and biotin, as well as the fermentation of complex carbohydrates that are otherwise indigestible. Beneficial bacteria, such as Lactobacillus species, also convert milk proteins into lactic acid in the gut. Additionally, the presence of these bacterial colonies inhibits the growth of potentially harmful bacteria through mechanisms like competitive exclusion. Some beneficial bacteria are marketed as probiotic dietary supplements. Although most bacteria are harmless or beneficial, certain pathogenic bacteria are responsible for infectious diseases. Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is the most common bacterial disease, killing approximately 2 million people annually, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. Other significant bacterial diseases include pneumonia, which can be caused by Streptococcus or Pseudomonas species, and foodborne illnesses caused by bacteria such as Shigella, Campylobacter, and Salmonella. Pathogenic bacteria are also responsible for diseases like tetanus, typhoid fever, diphtheria, syphilis, and leprosy. The criteria for establishing a causal relationship between a microbe and a disease were outlined by Robert Koch in 1890 and are known as Koch's postulates. In some cases, the pathogenic cause of a disease is discovered years later, as was the case with Helicobacter pylori and its role in peptic ulcer disease. Each pathogenic bacterial species interacts with human hosts in unique ways. For instance, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species can cause a range of infections, including skin infections, pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis. However, these bacteria are also part of the normal human flora and typically exist on the skin or in the nose without causing disease. In contrast, some bacteria, such as Rickettsia species, are obligate intracellular parasites that always cause disease. For example, one species of Rickettsia causes typhus, while another causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Similarly, Chlamydia species, another group of obligate intracellular parasites, can cause pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and may even be implicated in coronary heart disease. Certain bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia cenocepacia, and Mycobacterium avium, are opportunistic pathogens that primarily cause disease in individuals with weakened immune systems or conditions like cystic fibrosis. Bacterial infections are commonly treated with antibiotics, which are classified as either bactericidal (killing bacteria) or bacteriostatic (inhibiting bacterial growth). Different classes of antibiotics target specific processes in bacteria that differ from those in human cells, ensuring selective toxicity. For example, antibiotics like chloramphenicol and puromycin inhibit bacterial ribosomes without affecting eukaryotic ribosomes. Antibiotics are used not only to treat human diseases but also in intensive farming to promote animal growth. However, both uses contribute to the rapid emergence of antibiotic resistance in bacterial populations. Surgical and dental instruments are also sterilized to prevent contamination. Disinfectants like bleach are used to kill bacteria on surfaces, reducing the risk of infection. In food preparation, most bacteria are eliminated by cooking at temperatures above 60°C (140°F).
